headline: Healthcare and Software Lead a Broad Friday Rally, Leaving Chips and Homebuilders Behind
body_html:
Equities closed Friday's session on a constructive note, with 346 stocks advancing against 194 declining across the 544-name universe. Healthcare was the clear leader, gaining 1.45%, as investors rotated into defensive-growth names ahead of a week set to bring fresh earnings reports and inflation data. Software followed closely with a 1.03% advance, powered by a remarkable cluster of cloud and security names that surged in sympathy or on company-specific momentum. Materials, Industrials, and Energy posted modest positive prints, while Consumer was essentially flat.

The rotation told a pointed story: money moved away from semiconductors, which shed 0.48%, and Homebuilders bore the sharpest pain, sliding 1.44% as bond-market anxiety over rising yields continued to weigh on rate-sensitive groups. The day's standout mover was Hims & Hers Health, the telehealth platform, which surged 10.16% — the single largest advance in the universe. Cybersecurity firm Zscaler climbed 7.80%, while cloud-data specialist Snowflake and observability platform Datadog added 7.44% and 7.11% respectively, underscoring a concentrated bid for enterprise-software names with durable revenue models.

On the other side of the ledger, eXp World Holdings dropped 7.23%, Cirrus Logic fell 5.59%, and Fair Isaac retreated 5.57%, with the audio and RF chip names Cirrus Logic and Skyworks Solutions reinforcing the semiconductor sector's underperformance. With Wall Street positioned for weekly gains heading into the weekend, the opening question for Monday, October 12 is whether the bond market's unease — four warning signs of further yield pressure are already in circulation — will cap what has been a quietly resilient tech-and-healthcare tape.

briefs.headline: Telehealth Platform Posts Session's Biggest Gain Amid Healthcare Surge
briefs.body: Hims & Hers Health surged 10.16% on Friday, leading the entire universe and anchoring Healthcare's 1.45% advance. The move underscored renewed investor appetite for consumer-facing health-services companies, a corner of the market that had lagged for much of the prior quarter.

briefs.headline: Cloud and Security Names Stage Coordinated Advance
briefs.body: Zscaler, Snowflake, and Datadog each jumped more than 7% on Friday, lifting the Software sector to a 1.03% gain. Analysts have pointed to a broader recovery bid in high-multiple enterprise-technology stocks, with recent commentary suggesting institutional buyers are returning to names with durable recurring-revenue profiles.

briefs.headline: Semiconductor Stocks Retreat as Large Chip Trades Draw Scrutiny
briefs.body: The Semiconductors sector fell 0.48% on Friday, with Cirrus Logic and Skyworks Solutions each dropping more than 5%. The weakness arrived alongside reports of unusually large institutional block trades in major chip names, raising questions about whether smart money is repositioning ahead of an inflection in the cycle.

briefs.headline: Homebuilders Hit Hard as Bond-Market Alarm Bells Grow Louder
briefs.body: The Homebuilders sector was Friday's worst performer, shedding 1.44%, as rising Treasury yields continued to squeeze affordability assumptions. Market observers noted that at least four distinct technical and fundamental signals are now flashing caution on the bond market, a backdrop that historically pressures mortgage-rate-sensitive equities most acutely.

briefs.headline: Verizon Suffers Worst Single-Day Decline in More Than Two Decades
briefs.body: Shares of Verizon plummeted Friday after SpaceX disclosed plans to build a competing U.S. wireless network, sending shockwaves through the legacy telecom sector. The development was described as one of the most disruptive competitive threats to incumbent carriers in years, and the selloff rippled into other traditional telecom names.

briefs.headline: Tesla Quietly Retires 'Full Self-Driving' Label Across European Markets
briefs.body: Tesla has dropped the 'Full Self-Driving' brand name from its European product lineup following pressure from regional regulators who argued the term overstated the system's autonomous capabilities. The move marks a notable concession in the company's global marketing strategy and arrives as scrutiny of autonomous-driving claims intensifies among policymakers worldwide.
